usage: 산 takes adjective 높다, not 키가 크다 which is only for people/trees
에 marks the destination you head toward
I take photos on the mountain
에서 marks where an action happens, not movement
올라가다 (go up) is the verb of choice, not 오르다 alone in speech
examples: 저 산이 정말 높아요.
That mountain is really high.
Plain descriptive sentence; 이/가 spotlights 산 as the subject.
주말마다 산에 올라가요.
I climb the mountain every weekend.
에 marks the destination; 마다 means 'every', a common hiking-routine phrase.
가을에는 단풍 보러 산에 가는 사람이 많아요.
In autumn many people go to the mountain to see the fall foliage.
Real situation: 보러 가다 (go in order to see) plus the autumn-foliage culture.
nuance: 산 is the plain native word for a mountain or hill — Korea is about 70% mountainous, so 산 shows up constantly and even small wooded hills behind a neighborhood (뒷산, the back-hill) count as 산. The activity of climbing one is 등산(登山, literally 'ascend-mountain'), an enormously popular weekend hobby, so 등산하다/등산 가다 and 산에 올라가다 are everyday collocations. Watch the verb pairing: a mountain is 높다 (high), never 크다/키가 크다, and you climb it with 올라가다 rather than the bare 오르다 in casual speech. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'I go TO the mountain' tempts you toward 에서, but movement-toward always takes 에 (산에 가요); 에서 is reserved for an action performed AT the mountain (산에서 사진을 찍어요).

mistakes: Saying 산에서 가요 to mean 'I go to the mountain'. 에서 marks the place an action happens, not a destination, so for going there you must use 에: 산에 가요.
Calling a tall mountain 큰 산 by translating 'big' literally. Height of a mountain is 높다, so the natural phrase is 높은 산; 큰 산 sounds like it means broad/large in area, not tall.
Using 오르다 by itself in conversation like English 'climb'. Native speech prefers 산에 올라가요 (go up the mountain); bare 오르다 feels bookish.

usage: 바다 is 넓다 (wide) when stressing openness, 깊다 (deep) for depth
에서 marks where the swimming happens
take in the view; 바다 구경 = sea-sightseeing
examples: 바다가 정말 넓어요.
The sea is really wide.
Simple description; 이/가 makes 바다 the subject under focus.
여름에 바다에 놀러 가요.
In summer I go to the sea to have fun.
Everyday plan: 놀러 가다 = go in order to play/relax; 에 marks destination.
바다 보면서 회 한 접시 먹으면 최고예요.
Eating a plate of raw fish while looking at the sea is the best.
Real situation: 회(sashimi) + sea view is a beloved Korean coastal treat.
nuance: 바다 is the native word covering both 'sea' and 'ocean' — Korean doesn't routinely split the two, so 바다 does the work of both unless you specifically say 대양 (the technical 'ocean'). It's a top summer destination, tightly bound to 해수욕장 (海水浴場, 'sea-water-bathe-place', a swimming beach) and to 회 (raw fish) eaten by the shore. Describe it as 넓다 (wide) for its openness or 깊다 (deep) for depth, and pair it with 보다 (to look at / take in the view) for the scenic experience. The sharpest pitfall is sound-confusion: 바다 (sea) versus 바닥 (the floor/ground) differ by one final consonant, so 'sit on the floor' (바닥에 앉다) and 'go to the sea' (바다에 가다) are easy to swap — keep the final ㄱ of 바닥 audible. As with all destinations, going there is 바다에 가요 (에), while swimming AT it is 바다에서 수영해요 (에서).

Writing 바다에서 가요 for 'I go to the sea'. Movement toward a place takes 에, so it must be 바다에 가요; 에서 would wrongly mark it as the site of an action.

usage: a river is 길다 (long); 강물 = the river's water
I take a walk by the river
에서 marks where the walking happens
건너다 is the set verb for crossing water/roads
examples: 이 강은 아주 길어요.
This river is very long.
Simple description; a river's measure is 길다 (long).
저녁마다 강에서 산책해요.
I take a walk by the river every evening.
Everyday routine: 에서 marks the location of the walk, 마다 = every.
주말에 한강에서 치킨 시켜 먹는 게 국룰이에요.
Ordering and eating chicken by the Han River on weekends is the standard thing to do.
Real situation: 한강 picnics + delivery chicken; 국룰 = 'national rule', the default.
nuance: 강(江) is the Sino-Korean word for a river, the larger flowing-water term, as opposed to 시내/개울 (a small stream or brook) and 천(川) which names mid-size streams (e.g. 청계천). In Seoul, 강 almost reflexively evokes 한강 (the Han River), the city's iconic riverside park where people picnic, jog, bike, and order delivery food on the grass. A river is described as 길다 (long), its water is 강물, and the set verb for getting to the other side is 강을 건너다 (to cross). For English speakers the recurring trap is the particle contrast you'll meet with every place noun: 강에 가요 (에, going TO the river) versus 강에서 산책해요 (에서, the walk happens AT the river) — translating 'walk by the river' with the destination 에 is a classic slip. Also don't say 큰 강 expecting it to mean 'long'; size and length aren't the same adjective.

Translating 'cross the river' with 지나가다. The fixed verb for moving to the far bank is 건너다 — 강을 건너다 — while 지나가다 just means pass by.

usage: a tree IS 크다 (big/tall) — unlike a mountain, here 크다 is correct
아래 = under; 나무 밑 is the more casual equivalent
심다 is the dedicated verb for planting
examples: 저 나무가 정말 커요.
That tree is really big/tall.
Simple description; a tree, unlike a mountain, takes 크다 for size.
나무 아래에서 잠깐 쉬었어요.
I rested for a moment under the tree.
Everyday: 아래에서 = at the spot under it; 에서 marks where resting happens.
식목일에 가족이랑 같이 나무를 심었어요.
On Arbor Day I planted a tree together with my family.
Real situation: 식목일(Arbor Day) tree-planting; 심다 is the proper verb.
nuance: 나무 carries a useful double life: it means a living tree AND wood as a material (lumber), so 나무 책상 is a 'wooden desk' and 나무를 심다 is 'plant a tree' — context alone tells you which. It is the everyday native word; the Sino-Korean 목(木) survives only inside compounds like 목재 (timber) or 식목일 (Arbor Day, 植木日 'plant-tree-day'). A tree is described with 크다 (big/tall) — note the contrast with 산, which must use 높다 — and you 심다 (plant) it rather than any generic verb. The signature English-speaker mistake is treating plants like weather: 비가 와요 ('rain comes') tempts learners to say 나무가 와요, but a tree doesn't 오다; to talk about its growth use 자라다 (나무가 자라요, the tree grows). Also, 'under the tree' is 나무 아래/밑, with the location particle 에 or 에서 depending on whether something simply is there or an action occurs there.

usage: 꽃 is the prototypical 예쁘다 (pretty) noun
피다 is THE verb for blooming; 펴요 is its 요-form
꽃 takes 을/를 as an object; 꽃다발 = bouquet
also 꽃집; the place that sells flowers
examples: 이 꽃이 정말 예뻐요.
This flower is really pretty.
Simple compliment; 이/가 makes 꽃 the subject in focus.
봄이 되면 꽃이 활짝 펴요.
When spring comes, the flowers bloom fully.
Everyday: 활짝 (wide open) is the set adverb with 피다; 펴요 = blooms.
기념일이라 여자친구한테 꽃 한 다발 사 줬어요.
Since it was our anniversary, I bought my girlfriend a bouquet of flowers.
Real situation: 한 다발 = one bunch/bouquet; 한테 ... 사 주다 = buy for someone.
nuance: 꽃 is the native word for a flower or blossom, and the single most important thing to lock in is its verb partner: flowers 피다 (to bloom), so 꽃이 펴요 / 꽃이 피었어요 is how you say they are blooming/have bloomed — often intensified by 활짝 (활짝 피다, 'bloom wide open'). It pairs naturally with 예쁘다 (pretty) and 아름답다 (beautiful), and figures in gift culture: 꽃다발 (a bouquet), 꽃집/꽃 가게 (a flower shop), and giving 꽃을 주다 on anniversaries. The biggest pitfall mirrors the 나무 error — weather verbs don't transfer, so 꽃이 와요 is wrong; flowers don't 'come', they 피다. A second subtlety: the spelling 꽃 ends in ㅊ, and learners often mishear/mispronounce its liaisons — 꽃이 sounds like [꼬치], 꽃을 like [꼬츨] — so the consonant resurfaces before vowels even though final 꽃 alone is pronounced [꼳].

Treating 꽃 as uncountable like English and skipping a counter. To say a bouquet use 한 다발, for single stems 한 송이 — e.g. 장미 한 송이 (one rose).

usage: 풀 takes 푸르다, the 르 word that means vivid green/blue
there is a lot of grass
풀 + 밭(field); a patch of grass to sit on
뽑다 = pull out; weeding the yard
examples: 마당에 풀이 푸르러요.
The grass in the yard is green.
Simple description; 푸르다 conjugates to 푸르러요 (르 irregular).
우리는 풀밭에 앉아서 도시락을 먹었어요.
We sat on the grassy field and ate our packed lunch.
Everyday: 풀밭에 앉다 (sit on the lawn); 에 marks the spot of sitting.
여름엔 풀이 워낙 빨리 자라서 자주 깎아야 해요.
In summer the grass grows so fast that you have to mow it often.
Real situation: 자라다(grow) + 깎다(mow); 워낙 = 'by nature, extremely'.
nuance: 풀 is the native word for grass and, more broadly, low non-woody plants — which means it also covers 'weeds', the unwanted ones you 뽑다 (pull out) from a garden. The handy compound 풀밭 (풀 + 밭, 'grass-field') names a lawn or grassy patch where people sit and picnic. Its signature adjective is 푸르다 (vivid green/blue), a 르-irregular that becomes 푸르러요 (not 푸르어요), and it 자라다 (grows). Two traps await English speakers. First, homophone overload: 풀 also means 'glue/paste' (풀로 붙이다, stick with glue) and is the verb stem of 풀다 (to untie/solve) — only context separates them. Second, don't confuse 풀 (grass) with 숲 (forest): one is the low ground cover, the other the dense stand of trees. English lumps 'grass' as uncountable, so learners forget that for a single blade you'd say 풀 한 포기.

Saying 푸르어요 for the color. 푸르다 is a 르-irregular adjective, so the correct 요-form is 푸르러요 with a doubled ㄹ.

usage: a stone is sized with 크다; 무겁다 (heavy) is its other key adjective
던지다 = throw; 돌 is the object with 을/를
examples: 이 돌이 꽤 무거워요.
This stone is quite heavy.
Simple description; 무겁다 (heavy) is the natural adjective for 돌.
아이가 강에 돌을 던졌어요.
The child threw a stone into the river.
Everyday: 던지다 takes 을/를; 강에 = into the river (destination 에).
제주도엔 돌담으로 둘러싸인 옛날 집이 많아요.
On Jeju Island there are many old houses surrounded by stone walls.
Real situation: 돌담(stone wall) culture; 둘러싸이다 = be surrounded.
nuance: 돌 is the native word for a stone or rock — the everyday term, while 석(石) and 암(巖) are Sino-Korean elements living inside compounds like 석탑 (stone pagoda) or 암석 (rock, geological). It builds vivid compounds such as 돌담 (stone wall) and 돌다리 (stone bridge), staples of old Korean villages, and on volcanic Jeju the 돌하르방 (grandfather statues) are carved from it. A stone is described as 크다 (big) and especially 무겁다 (heavy), and you 던지다 (throw) it or 줍다 (pick it up). The notable pitfall is a homonym that's culturally loaded: 돌 also means a baby's first birthday (the 돌잔치, first-birthday party). They're spelled identically, so 돌이 무거워요 (the stone is heavy) and 돌이 지났어요 (the first birthday has passed) rely entirely on context. English speakers also tend to over-distinguish 'stone' from 'rock', but 돌 comfortably covers both the pebble and the rock.

Using 무겁다 to mean 'hard'. 무겁다 is heavy (weight); if you mean the stone is hard to the touch, that's 단단하다. Don't conflate the two.

usage: an island is sized with 작다/크다
들어가다 'enter' is idiomatic for reaching an island
examples: 저 섬이 아주 작아요.
That island is very small.
Simple description; 이/가 makes 섬 the subject in focus.
배를 타고 섬에 들어갔어요.
I went over to the island by boat.
Everyday: 배를 타다 (take a boat) + 섬에 들어가다, the natural 'reach an island'.
할머니는 평생 그 섬에서 혼자 사셨어요.
Grandmother lived alone on that island her whole life.
Real situation: 에서 marks where she lived; 사시다 is the honorific of 살다.
nuance: 섬 is the pure native word for an island. The Sino-Korean counterpart is 도(島), which doesn't stand alone but attaches to island names — 제주도 (Jeju Island), 울릉도, 독도 — so the -도 you hear in those names literally means 'island'. A handy idiom: to 'go to an island' Koreans often say 섬에 들어가다 (literally 'enter the island'), as if stepping into a separate world, and to leave is 섬에서 나오다. Islands are reached 배를 타고 (by boat) and described with 작다/크다. The usual particle pitfall applies — destination 섬에 가요 (에) versus the place of an action 섬에서 살아요 (에서) — and the 'I go TO the island' phrasing in English tempts the wrong 에서. Don't double up by saying '제주도 섬', since 도 already means island; just say 제주도, or 제주 섬 informally.

Saying 제주도 섬, which is redundant. The 도 in 제주도 already means 'island' (島), so just say 제주도; adding 섬 doubles the meaning.
Using 가다 with no helper verb when boarding for an island and expecting it to sound natural. Koreans idiomatically say 섬에 들어가다 (enter the island); plain 섬에 가다 is fine too but 들어가다 is more vivid.

usage: a lake is 넓다 (wide) for surface, 깊다 for depth
I ride a boat on the lake
에서 marks where the boating happens
examples: 이 호수가 정말 넓어요.
This lake is really wide.
Simple description; surface size of a lake is 넓다 (wide).
아침에 호수 주변을 한 바퀴 돌았어요.
In the morning I walked one loop around the lake.
Everyday: 한 바퀴 돌다 = go around once, a common walking phrase.
가을엔 호수에 물안개가 껴서 진짜 분위기 있어요.
In autumn, mist settles on the lake and it's really atmospheric.
Real situation: 물안개가 끼다 (mist forms); 분위기 있다 = has a nice mood.
nuance: 호수(湖水) is a Sino-Korean compound literally meaning 'lake-water' (湖 lake + 水 water) — a still, land-enclosed body of water, contrasted with the flowing 강 (river) and the vast 바다 (sea). The key contrast for learners: 호수 is calm and bounded, whereas 강 moves and 바다 is open and salty; choosing among them is about the water's form, not just size. A lake is 넓다 (wide across) or 깊다 (deep), its edge is 호숫가 (the lakeside, note the inserted ㅅ), and people 보트를 타다 (ride a boat) or stroll 호수 주변 (around it). The same destination-vs-location particle rule governs everything: 호수에 가요 (에, going there) but 호수에서 보트를 타요 (에서, the boating happens there). Because 호수 is fully Sino-Korean and a bit formal, in casual speech for a small pond you might instead hear 연못 (a garden pond) — don't call a tiny ornamental pond a 호수.

Mixing up 호수 (lake, still water) with 강 (river, flowing water). They're different bodies of water — a lake is enclosed and calm, a river flows — so they aren't interchangeable.

usage: 숲 is 깊다 (deep) when dense, 우거지다 (overgrown) for lushness
I take a walk in the forest
에서 marks where the walking happens
숲 + 속(inside); the interior of the woods
examples: 이 숲은 정말 깊어요.
This forest is really deep.
Simple description; a dense forest is 깊다 (deep), as if hard to see through.
숲에서 새소리를 들으니까 마음이 편해졌어요.
Hearing birdsong in the forest, my mind grew calm.
Everyday: 에서 marks where the hearing happens; 새소리 = birdsong.
요즘 사람들이 힐링하러 숲속 캠핑을 많이 가요.
These days many people go forest camping to recharge.
Real situation: 힐링(healing/recharge) + 숲속 캠핑; the nature-wellness trend.
nuance: 숲 is the native word for a forest or woods — a stand of many trees thick enough to feel enclosed — and pairs with 깊다 (deep, when dense) or 우거지다 (to grow lush/overgrown). Its essential compound is 숲속 (숲 + 속, 'inside the forest'), meaning the quiet interior where you're surrounded by trees; 숲길 is a forest path. It carries a calm, restorative connotation, riding the popular 힐링(healing) and 숲세권 (living near woods) trends. Two pitfalls: spelling/sound — 숲 ends in ㅍ, so although bare 숲 is pronounced [숩], the consonant resurfaces in 숲이 [수피], 숲에서 [수페서]; and a recurring mix-up with 풀 (grass) — 숲 is the dense woods of tall trees, 풀 is the low grass underfoot, so don't swap them. Scale also matters: a couple of trees is just 나무 몇 그루, not yet a 숲; the word implies a real expanse of woodland.

Pronouncing 숲에 as [수베] or dropping the consonant. The final ㅍ links to the vowel, so 숲에 = [수페] and 숲이 = [수피]; 숲 alone is [숩].
Calling a few scattered trees a 숲. 숲 implies a real expanse of dense woodland; for just a handful of trees say 나무 몇 그루 (a few trees) instead.

usage: a star is 밝다 (bright); also 반짝이다 (twinkle)
뜨다 is the verb; 떠요 / 떴어요 are its forms
there are many stars in the sky
examples: 오늘 밤은 별이 참 밝아요.
Tonight the stars are really bright.
Simple description; a star's quality is 밝다 (bright).
밤이 되니까 하늘에 별이 떴어요.
As night fell, the stars came out in the sky.
Everyday: 뜨다 → 떴어요 (came out); 에 marks where they appear.
시골 가면 별이 쏟아질 듯이 많아서 진짜 장관이에요.
In the countryside there are so many stars it's like they'll pour down — a real spectacle.
Real situation: 쏟아질 듯이 (as if pouring); 장관 = magnificent sight.
nuance: 별 is the native word for a star, and its crucial verb partner is 뜨다 (to rise/come out) — the very same verb used for the sun and moon — so 별이 떠요 / 별이 떴어요 means stars appear, and they set with 지다 (별이 지다). It's described as 밝다 (bright) and 반짝이다 (to twinkle), and figures in fixed phrases like 별을 보다 (stargaze) and the metaphor 별 (a 'star' = celebrity, same as English) plus 별점 (star rating). The leading pitfall is verb choice: English 'the stars come out' lures learners into 별이 와요, but stars don't 오다 — and weather-style 비가 와요 doesn't transfer here either; the right verb is 뜨다. Note too the homophone-ish 벌 (a bee / a punishment): 별 with the ㅕ vowel is a star, 벌 with ㅓ is a bee — keep the vowels distinct so 별 받다 doesn't come out as 벌 받다 ('be punished').

Confusing 별 (star) with 벌 (bee / punishment). The vowels differ — 별 has ㅕ, 벌 has ㅓ — so 벌을 받다 means 'get punished', nothing to do with stars. Keep the vowel clear.
Using 빛나다 and 반짝이다 interchangeably without care. Both relate to shining, but 반짝이다 specifically captures the twinkling/flickering of stars; 빛나다 is a steadier 'glow/shine'.

usage: the moon is 밝다 (bright); 둥근 달 = round moon
뜨다 is the verb; 떠요 / 떴어요 are its forms
there is a moon in the sky
보름(15th, mid-month) + 달; the round full moon
examples: 오늘 밤 달이 참 밝네요.
The moon is really bright tonight.
Simple remark; 밝다 (bright) + the soft observing ending -네요.
저녁이 되니까 동쪽에서 달이 떴어요.
As evening came, the moon rose in the east.
Everyday: 뜨다 → 떴어요; 동쪽에서 = from the east (where it rises).
추석에는 보름달 보면서 소원을 빌어요.
On Chuseok we make a wish while looking at the full moon.
Real situation: 추석(harvest festival) + 보름달; 소원을 빌다 = make a wish.
nuance: 달 carries two everyday meanings — the moon AND a calendar month (한 달 = one month, 다음 달 = next month) — so the same syllable is one of Korean's classic double-duty words, disambiguated purely by context. As the celestial moon it 뜨다 (rises) and 지다 (sets), exactly like 해 (sun) and 별 (star), giving 달이 떴어요; it's 밝다 (bright) and 둥글다 (round). Culturally it anchors 보름달 (보름 'the 15th/mid-month' + 달 = full moon), central to 추석 (the harvest festival) when families 소원을 빌다 (make wishes) under it. Pitfalls: first, the verb — don't say 달이 와요 ('the moon comes'); the moon 뜨다, not 오다. Second, beware the month/moon overlap: 달이 떴어요 = 'the moon rose', but 두 달 = 'two months' (counted with the native-number+달), and 한 달 means a month, never 'one moon'. Keep the context cue in mind so the two senses don't collide.
